name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
answer: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is the structured review of how an organisation's finance function actually uses artificial intelligence, covering the tools in play, the data feeding them, the controls around them and the evidence trail they leave. It sits inside governance, risk and financial data security, and it is the point where an internal audit plan meets the AI systems that touch ledgers, forecasts, reconciliations and reporting. The audit is not a test of model accuracy alone, it asks whether the use of AI in finance is authorised, documented and defensible.

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is the structured review of how an organisation's finance function actually uses artificial intelligence, covering the tools in play, the data feeding them, the controls around them and the evidence trail they leave. It sits inside governance, risk and financial data security, and it is the point where an internal audit plan meets the AI systems that touch ledgers, forecasts, reconciliations and reporting. The audit is not a test of model accuracy alone, it asks whether the use of AI in finance is authorised, documented and defensible.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit draws on the finance stack as it stands: enterprise resource planning systems, reporting and consolidation platforms, spreadsheets, and the growing set of AI tools that sit alongside or inside them. It also depends on the organisation's own records, including model inventories, vendor contracts, data flow maps, access logs and change history. Where AI features are embedded in existing finance software, the audit has to reach the vendor's documentation and assurance reports, because much of the control evidence lives outside the company's own walls.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work begins with scoping, which means identifying every AI use in finance, from forecasting and anomaly detection to document processing and narrative drafting, and separating sanctioned tools from shadow use. Auditors then walk the lifecycle: how data is selected and prepared, who approves a model or tool, how outputs are reviewed before they reach a ledger or a filing, and how errors are logged and corrected. Testing combines interviews, sample-based transaction checks, control walkthroughs and review of model documentation, with findings rated and tracked to remediation. The output is a report that states what is enabled, what is controlled and what remains unproven.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on accountability: who owns each AI use in finance, what the vendor is permitted to do with the data, and whether personal or material non-public information is exposed. Provenance matters because an AI-generated figure in a forecast or disclosure has to be traceable to its source data and to the person who approved it. The audit tests this against internal policy and against the regulatory expectations the firm is subject to, and it records gaps rather than resolving them. Nothing in an audit of this kind is legal, financial or investment advice, and findings are evidence for management and the board, not instructions to a reader.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect the audit to move from periodic review toward continuous monitoring, with automated checks on model use, data access and output review built into finance workflows. Regulators are asking for more documented oversight of AI in reporting and decision making, and vendors are adding assurance material to keep pace. The practical direction is a standing inventory of AI use in finance, refreshed as tools change, so that the audit question shifts from whether AI is used to whether its use can be evidenced on demand.
